newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq says U.S. delaying arrival of food, medicine.
newsitem.headline: Iraq says U.S. delaying arrival of food, medicine.

text.p: Iraq on Friday denied claims by the United States that it was delaying the arrival of food and medical supplies to its own people.

"Everybody knows well that the American envoy (at the U.N. sanctions committee) is the reason for the delay of the arrival of foodstuffs and medicines to Iraq," a foreign ministry source said in a statement reported by the official Iraqi News Agency (INA).

Under the "oil-for-food" agreement between Iraq and the United Nations, which entered into force on Dec. 10, Baghdad is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy humanitarian items to mitigate the effects of sanctions in force since Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Iraq says no food or medical shipments under the deal have reached its territory yet.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns acknowledged the delays on Monday but attributed the main reason to Baghdad's insistence to deny U.N. monitors the full freedom of movement it promised to give under the deal.
"This is getting to be farcical...If anyone is to blame for U.N. resolution 986's slowness it is the Iraqi government themselves," Burns said.
The Iraqi spokesman accused Burns of lying and said "U.N. officials before others viewed his remarks with derision."

"Coordination between the concerned Iraqi authorities and the U.N. Secretariat General and U.N. coordinator's office in Baghdad takes place every day....There is full coordination to start the implementation of the memorandum of understanding once the foodstuffs and medicines arrive in Iraq," he said.
Diplomats in Baghdad said earlier the two sides were still haggling over the duties of U.N. monitors, particularly their freedom of movement, communications gear and means of transport.
U.N. relief officials in Baghdad declined comment on Friday and the Iraqi source made no mention of these problems.

The source said Iraq had submitted more than 120 contracts for the purchase of food and medicine since the deal went through but only four of them passed the sanctions committee due to hurdles placed by the U.S. envoy.
